common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 - Removing the multiple-provider error lets a FIPS setup silently run on a non-FIPS provider.. Before this change, finding more than one `CryptoProvider` was a hard error. Now the providers are sorted by `order()` and the first one wins. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider` and `WildFlyElytronProvider` all return 200, so when both the default and the FIPS jars are on the classpath (a common packaging mistake), the sort keeps ServiceLoader's classpath order. The non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider can then be chosen, and the only trace is a debug log line. A FIPS deployment that used to fail fast now quietly uses non-compliant crypto.

Fix: still throw (or at least log a warning) when two or more providers share the highest order. Only allow picking by order when there is a single highest provider, such as the authz-client fallback at 100.

The return statement right below builds both again. These look like leftovers; remove the two lines.

authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 - The ES384 and ES512 tests sign with a P-256 key, so they never test those curves' sizes.. `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` uses the JDK's default curve, which is P-256. That means r and s are always 32 bytes or fewer, even in the ES384 and ES512 tests. The 48- and 66-byte paths in `integerToBytes` and `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` are only checked with small values, so a size-handling bug for P-384 or P-521 would still pass. Fix: initialize the generator with the matching curve for each algorithm (`secp256r1`, `secp384r1`, `secp521r1`).
